findings.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — Exact, case-sensitive lookup lets users bypass an email block by changing email casing.
lib/validators/email_validator.rb:20 — Domain regex is not anchored at the end, so a whitelist entry for example.com also accepts user@example.com.attacker.org.
app/models/blocked_email.rb:14-16 — `match_count += 1` followed by `save` is a non-atomic read-modify-write; concurrent validations can undercount matches and regress `last_match_at`.

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

per_golden_matches.reasoning: Both comments identify the same underlying issue: the `should_block_email?` method has problematic side effects (updating match_count and last_match_at via save) during what appears to be a read/check operation. The golden comment emphasizes the misleading method name and side effects during read, while the candidate focuses on the race condition/concurrency aspect. Both point to the same code problem - the non-atomic update operation that can cause race conditions in concurrent environments.

per_golden_matches.matched_candidate: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:20 — Domain regex is not anchored at the end, so a whitelist entry for example.com also accepts user@example.com.attacker.org.
per_golden_matches.reasoning: Both comments identify the same underlying security issue: the domain regex pattern is not properly anchored, allowing domain suffix matching instead of exact domain matching. The golden comment describes it as matching 'domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring' where 'evil.example.com' could bypass 'example.com'. The candidate describes it as 'not anchored at the end' where 'example.com.attacker.org' could bypass 'example.com'. While the specific bypass examples differ slightly (subdomain prefix vs domain suffix attack), both identify the same core vulnerability: improper regex anchoring in domain validation that allows bypass of domain restrictions.
